cards.front: Name the 7 OSI layers from bottom to top.
cards.back: Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application. ("Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away.")

cards.front: Which OSI layer do routers and IP addresses work at?
cards.back: Layer 3, Network.

cards.front: Which OSI layer do switches and MAC addresses work at?
cards.back: Layer 2, Data Link.

cards.front: TCP and UDP belong to which OSI layer?
cards.back: Layer 4, Transport.

cards.front: DNS port?
cards.back: 53 (UDP for most queries, TCP for zone transfers and large responses).

cards.front: DHCP ports?
cards.back: UDP 67 (server) and 68 (client).

cards.front: SMTP, POP3 and IMAP ports?
cards.back: SMTP 25 (587 for submission). POP3 110, or 995 over TLS. IMAP 143, or 993 over TLS.

cards.front: RDP port?
SNMP ports?
cards.back: UDP 161 (queries) and 162 (traps).

cards.front: LDAP and LDAPS ports?
cards.back: LDAP 389, LDAPS 636.

cards.front: SMB port?
cards.back: TCP 445.

cards.front: NTP port?
cards.back: UDP 123.

cards.front: Syslog port?
cards.back: UDP 514 (TCP 514 or 6514 with TLS in some setups).

cards.front: FTP, SFTP and TFTP ports?
cards.back: FTP 20/21. SFTP runs over SSH on 22. TFTP UDP 69.

cards.front: The three private IPv4 ranges?
What does a 169.254.x.x address mean?
cards.back: APIPA: the device could not get an address from DHCP and assigned itself a link-local address.

cards.front: IPv4 loopback and IPv6 loopback?
IPv6 link-local prefix?
How many usable hosts in a /26?
cards.back: 62 (64 addresses minus network and broadcast).

cards.front: What is NAT / PAT?
cards.back: Network Address Translation maps private addresses to public ones. PAT (overload) lets many devices share one public IP using different ports.

cards.front: Describe the DHCP process.
cards.back: DORA: Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge.

cards.front: What DNS record maps an IP back to a name?
cards.back: PTR (reverse lookup).

cards.front: What do A, AAAA and CNAME records do?
cards.back: A maps a name to IPv4, AAAA to IPv6, CNAME aliases one name to another.

cards.front: What standard tags VLANs on a trunk?
cards.back: IEEE 802.1Q.

cards.front: What does Spanning Tree Protocol prevent?
cards.back: Switching loops (and the broadcast storms they cause) by blocking redundant paths.

cards.front: What is link aggregation (LACP)?
cards.back: Combining several physical links into one logical link for bandwidth and redundancy (IEEE 802.3ad / 802.1AX).

cards.front: PoE standards and power at the switch port?
cards.back: 802.3af up to 15.4 W, 802.3at (PoE+) up to 30 W, 802.3bt up to 60 W (Type 3) or 90 W (Type 4).

cards.front: OSPF is what type of routing protocol?
cards.back: Link-state (interior gateway protocol).

cards.front: Which routing protocol runs the internet between organizations?
cards.back: BGP, a path-vector exterior gateway protocol.

cards.front: RIP's maximum hop count?
cards.back: 15 (16 means unreachable). RIP is distance-vector.

cards.front: Which Wi-Fi generation is 802.11ax, and what does 6E add?
cards.back: Wi-Fi 6. Wi-Fi 6E adds the 6 GHz band.

cards.front: What does WPA3-Personal use instead of a pre-shared key handshake?
cards.back: SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals), which resists offline password guessing.

cards.front: Non-overlapping 2.4 GHz channels in the US?
Max length of twisted-pair Ethernet run?
cards.back: 100 meters.

cards.front: Single-mode vs multimode fiber?
cards.back: Single-mode: thin core, laser, long distances. Multimode: wider core, shorter distances, cheaper optics.

cards.front: Which tool finds which wall jack a cable goes to?
cards.back: A toner and probe.

cards.front: CompTIA troubleshooting method, in order?
cards.back: Identify the problem, establish a theory, test the theory, establish a plan, implement or escalate, verify full functionality, document findings.

cards.front: Which command shows the path packets take on Windows?
cards.back: tracert (traceroute on Linux/macOS).

cards.front: Which command shows a host's IP-to-MAC (ARP) table?
cards.back: arp -a.

cards.front: What is 802.1X?
cards.back: Port-based network access control: devices must authenticate (often via RADIUS) before getting network access.

cards.front: DDR4 vs DDR5: can they swap slots?
cards.back: No. They are keyed differently and are not compatible.

cards.front: What is NVMe?
cards.back: A protocol for SSDs over PCIe, much faster than SATA. Common in the M.2 form factor.

cards.front: RAID 0, 1, 5 and 10?
cards.back: 0: striping, no redundancy. 1: mirroring. 5: striping with parity, survives one disk failure (min 3 disks). 10: mirrored stripes (min 4 disks).

cards.front: What does POST do?
cards.back: Power-On Self-Test checks core hardware before the operating system loads.

cards.front: What is a TPM used for?
cards.back: A chip that stores keys securely; used by BitLocker, Secure Boot measurements and Windows 11 requirements.

cards.front: Prevent ESD damage when working inside a PC?
cards.back: Use an anti-static wrist strap and mat, and handle components by the edges.

cards.front: The steps of the laser printing process?
cards.back: Processing, charging, exposing, developing, transferring, fusing, cleaning.

cards.front: Which printer type uses heat on special paper and has no ink?
cards.back: Thermal (common for receipts and labels).

cards.front: Command that checks and repairs Windows system files?
cards.back: sfc /scannow.

cards.front: Command to check a disk for errors?
cards.back: chkdsk (chkdsk /f to fix).

cards.front: Command that refreshes Group Policy?
cards.back: gpupdate /force (gpresult shows what applied).

cards.front: Copy large folders reliably with retries from the command line?
cards.back: robocopy.

cards.front: Where do you look for application crashes and logon failures?
cards.back: Event Viewer (eventvwr.msc).

cards.front: Which tool changes startup items and boot options (classic)?
cards.back: msconfig (startup apps now live in Task Manager).

cards.front: NTFS vs FAT32 vs exFAT?
cards.back: NTFS: Windows default, permissions, encryption, large files. FAT32: universal but 4 GB file limit. exFAT: removable drives, large files, no NTFS permissions.

cards.front: Workgroup vs domain?
cards.back: Workgroup: each PC manages its own accounts. Domain: accounts and policy are managed centrally by Active Directory.

cards.front: macOS backup tool and disk encryption?
cards.back: Time Machine for backups, FileVault for full-disk encryption.

cards.front: Linux command to install packages on Debian/Ubuntu?
cards.back: sudo apt install <package> (after sudo apt update).

cards.front: Type 1 vs Type 2 hypervisor?
cards.back: Type 1 runs directly on hardware (bare metal, e.g. ESXi, Hyper-V). Type 2 runs on top of an OS (e.g. VirtualBox).

cards.front: IaaS vs PaaS vs SaaS?
cards.back: IaaS: rent servers and networks. PaaS: rent a platform to run your code. SaaS: use finished software, like email.

cards.front: The CompTIA malware removal steps?
cards.back: Investigate and verify symptoms; quarantine the system; disable System Restore (Windows); remediate (update tools, scan, remove); schedule scans and updates; re-enable System Restore and create a restore point; educate the user.

cards.front: First things to change on a new SOHO router?
cards.back: Default admin password, firmware updates, WPA3 (or WPA2-AES), disable WPS and remote admin, change the default network name.

cards.front: What is MDM?
cards.back: Mobile device management: central control of phones and tablets (policies, apps, remote wipe).

cards.front: The 3-2-1 backup rule?
cards.back: Three copies of data, on two kinds of media, with one copy offsite (or offline).

cards.front: Why use change management?
cards.back: To plan, approve, test and document changes so they do not cause unexpected outages, with a rollback plan.

cards.front: What should a good help desk ticket include?
cards.back: User and contact info, device, clear problem description, steps tried, priority, and resolution notes.

cards.front: What is the safest way to dispose of an old hard drive with sensitive data?
cards.back: Physical destruction or certified wiping/shredding with a certificate of destruction.
